RagShortTexts: The Order of Santiago bore red sword-crosses, safeguarding the pilgrimage route to Compostela.

Variants.Content: The Order of Santiago took its name from Saint James, the apostle venerated as the Moor-slayer in Castilian tradition. Its knights wore the red sword-cross, and the order admitted the sons of Castilian and Leonese nobility, who then took vows under the Augustinian rule. Its duties were twofold. It guarded the pilgrim road to Compostela, where hospices and bridges depended on order-held properties, and it held frontier pastures in Extremadura that fed its horses and men. The order's wealth came from those lands and from royal grants, and that wealth paid for the knights who rode with the crown.

The Grand Master of Santiago commanded revenues that rivalled those of the royal domains. The order blended secular inheritance with the brotherhood of a religious order, and its knights kept the Augustinian rule that allowed married men to serve. That mix let it field disciplined divisions during royal sieges in Andalusia.
Pilgrim hospices and bridges along the Camino are sustained by Santiago commanderies. When mountain brigands strike unwary travelers, knights ride out promptly to hang culprits along roadsides.
